pedagogy.summary: Children measure area by covering a figure with unit squares and counting them — in square centimetres, square metres, square inches or square feet — including irregular and L-shaped figures, and compare two shapes by their counts. The counting must be of the squares that COVER the interior with no gaps or overlaps (not the boundary), done systematically so every square is counted once, with the answer stated in square units.
bestPractices: Cover the whole interior with unit squares, no gaps or overlaps, and count the covering squares — not the squares around the edge.
Count systematically (row by row, or decompose an L-shape into rectangles) so no square is missed or double-counted.
Use real square-unit tiles (square-centimetre tiles on a book cover) before squared-paper diagrams.
Compare areas of two shapes directly by their counts.
Always state the area in square units (square cm, square m).
Keep to whole unit squares at this stage; treat part-squares informally rather than with a formula.
keyRepresentations: Square-centimetre tiles covering a book cover
L-shaped and irregular figures on squared paper
A shape decomposed into rectangles for systematic counting
A count recorded with its square unit (e.g. '18 square cm')
commonMisconceptions: Counts the squares around the boundary (perimeter) instead of the squares covering the interior.
Leaves gaps or overlaps, or counts unsystematically so squares are missed or double-counted (especially on L-shapes).
Counts every partly-covered square at the edge as a whole square, overestimating.
Gives the count as a bare number without the square unit.

learn.summary: Children measure area by covering a figure's interior with unit squares — no gaps or overlaps — and counting the covering squares systematically, stating the answer in square units (square cm, square m, square in, square ft). Work includes irregular and L-shaped figures (decomposed into rectangles), comparing two shapes by their counts, and telling the area (every covering square, including the squares along the inner edge) apart from the length of the boundary (unit lengths around the outline, i.e. perimeter) and from a count of only the border squares. Concrete tiles on a real surface precede squared-paper diagrams. Keep to whole unit squares at this stage, treating edge part-squares informally.

activities.title: Tile and count an L-shaped garden
feedback: If a child counts only the squares along the border, point out that the border squares are part of the covering but the squares further in must be counted too; shade the whole interior, border squares included, and recount every covering square. If they count unit lengths around the outline instead, explain that this is the distance around (perimeter), not the area.
If tiles leave gaps or overlap, or recounting gives a different total, cover fully with no gaps/overlaps and count row by row or by decomposing into rectangles, marking each square as it is counted.
If they lose track in the L's notch, decompose the L into two rectangles and count each separately, then add.
If they give '18' with no unit, treat the answer as incomplete and build the habit of naming the square unit — the counting itself is sound.
activities.rationale: Covering a region with no gaps or overlaps and counting the whole unit squares, including decomposing rectilinear (L-shaped) figures into rectangles, is the Grade-3 area practice described in the source progressions. Making the systematic covering the act the child performs targets the gap/overlap and edge-counting difficulties directly.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.

When iterating units children may leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering a region with no gaps; L-shaped (rectilinear) figures are decomposed into rectangles, and coordinating the covering requires spatial structuring that develops with many array activities.
learnerActions: Cover an L-shaped figure's whole interior with unit squares so there are no gaps and no overlaps, including the awkward squares inside the notch of the L.
Count the covering squares systematically — row by row, or by splitting the L into two rectangles and counting each — marking each square as you count it so none is missed or double-counted.
State the result in square units, e.g. '18 square cm' or in square metres, not just a bare number.
Repeat with a plain rectangle and then compare two shapes side by side, deciding which covers more by comparing their counts.
activities.intendedInsight: Area is the count of unit squares that cover the inside of a shape — notches and all — and is about the surface inside, not the fence or distance running around the edge.

activities.title: Tile a real surface before squared paper
feedback: If tiles overlap or leave bare patches, rearrange so they tile the surface completely and evenly before counting.
If the paper-diagram count differs from the count of physical tiles, line the two up and check that each paper square stands for exactly one tile.
activities.rationale: The progressions describe starting from covering with a two-dimensional unit; using real square-unit tiles on a concrete surface before abstract squared-paper diagrams is intended to ground the covering idea, though the cited sources do not establish the ordering's comparative efficacy.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.
learnerActions: Lay square-centimetre tiles across a small real surface such as a book cover, filling it with no gaps or overlaps; if strips narrower than a tile are left at the edges, note them informally as part-squares rather than counting them as whole tiles.
Count the tiles and say the area in square centimetres.
Then move to a squared-paper diagram of the same shape drawn at the same size (one paper square for each tile) and count the covering squares there.
activities.intendedInsight: Measuring area means physically covering a surface with equal square units and counting them; the squared-paper diagram is a picture of that same covering.

activities.title: Compare and check with quick counting questions
feedback: If a child picks the answer that comes from counting only the border squares, show that the inside squares were left out: the area includes every covering square, the border squares and the ones further in.
For part-squares at an edge, discuss them informally — do not count every touched square as a whole one, and do not apply a formula at this stage.
activities.rationale: Checking understanding with comparison and count items, including an edge-counting distractor, surfaces the boundary-counting difficulty; such questions verify understanding rather than build the systematic covering, so pair them with hands-on tiling. The part-square figure is used for discussion, not a scored count, because whole-square counting is the Grade-3 focus.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.
learnerActions: Given two shapes on squared paper, decide which covers more area by counting each one's squares.

Answer a short set of count-the-squares questions using whole-square figures — a plain rectangle and an L-shape, each with a definite count — then separately look at one shape with part-squares at the edge and discuss (rather than score) how to handle the part-squares informally.

Watch for a tempting wrong answer that comes from counting only the border squares (or the unit lengths around the outline) instead of all the squares covering the inside, and explain why it is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing areas means comparing counts of all the covering squares, edge squares included; counting only the border squares does not give the area, and the distance around the outline (perimeter) is a different thing from the area inside.

activities.title: Read a finished counted figure
feedback: Use this reference to contrast with a child's own counting — ask them to point to any square they counted that the reference did not, and discuss.
activities.rationale: A static filled figure with the count shown illustrates the target result and can prompt discussion, but it cannot rehearse the systematic gap-free counting itself, so it serves as a worked reference rather than the main practice.
learnerActions: Study a figure already filled with unit squares and its revealed count, e.g. '18 square cm'.
Retrace which squares were counted and confirm every square inside the outline, including those along the edge, is counted exactly once, and nothing outside the outline is counted.
Say back how the count and unit were obtained.
activities.intendedInsight: A completed, correctly counted figure models what a finished area measurement looks like: every interior square counted once, with the square unit named.

constraints: Count every square that covers the inside of the outline, with no gaps or overlaps — including the squares along the edge, which are part of the area. Do not count only the border squares, and do not count squares outside the outline. The distance around the outline (perimeter, measured in unit lengths) is a different kind of quantity from an area count.
Count systematically (row by row, or by decomposing an L-shape into rectangles) so each square is counted exactly once.
Always state the area in square units (square cm, square m, etc.); a bare number is an incomplete answer.

Keep to whole unit squares at this stage; treat edge part-squares informally (e.g. pairing two halves) and do NOT drill a part-square formula yet — part-square figures are for discussion, not scored counts.
Real tiles and squared-paper diagrams each support learning differently — tiles ground the physical covering, diagrams abstract it; neither is claimed as universally necessary.
A revealed static figure is a reference/scaffold: it shows the result but does not let the child practise the covering and counting, so it should not replace hands-on tiling.
A count-the-squares check verifies understanding and can catch edge-counting, but does not by itself build the systematic covering skill.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row framed the boundary-counting misconception as a total that 'matches the perimeter'. A count of boundary squares is not generally equal to the perimeter (a length); learner-facing text uses an inside-vs-around distinction without asserting a numeric match. This original imprecision was not re-verified against sources.

The source row rated a 3D scene 'poor' (risk of conflating area with volume) and a conversation 'poor'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than asserted as universal claims. A spoken discussion of what was counted remains valuable (see the probe questions).

Interactive affordances from the source (tiles greying out when counted to prevent double-counting, uncovered cells flashing, a running square-unit tally, side-by-side compare mode) are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory requirements.

The source claim supports covering with a two-dimensional unit but does not directly establish the concrete-tiles-before-diagram ordering's efficacy; that ordering is retained as curriculum best practice with hedged wording.

'18 square cm' is used only as an illustrative label, not a computed answer to verify; boundary vs interior counting, no-gaps/no-overlaps covering, L-shape decomposition, and informal handling of part-squares (as discussion rather than scored counts) are internally consistent.

probeDeeper: Show me which squares you counted — the ones inside the shape, or the ones around the edge?
This L-shape — how did you make sure you counted every square once and none twice?
There are some half-squares at the edge here — what did you do with those?
You said 18 — 18 what? What is the unit for area?
assess.correctAnswer: The child covers each interior with unit squares (no gaps or overlaps) and counts them systematically — decomposing the L-shape so every square is counted once — gives the count in square units (e.g. '18 square cm'), handles edge part-squares sensibly rather than as whole units, and compares two shapes by their counts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the boundary, not the interior: counts squares around the edge (perimeter) rather than the squares covering the surface.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to what area means — the surface covered; shade the interior and count only covering squares, contrasting with the distance around.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to and counts the squares along the border; the total matches the perimeter, not the area.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gaps/overlaps or unsystematic counting: covers with gaps or overlaps, or counts without a system so squares are missed or double-counted, especially on the L-shape.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cover fully with no gaps/overlaps and count row by row or by decomposing into rectangles, marking each square as counted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tiles don't fully cover or overlap; recounting gives a different total; loses track in the L's notch.

errorPatterns.pattern: Part-squares counted as whole: counts each partly-covered edge square as a full square, overestimating the area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill a part-square formula at this stage — Grade-3 area focuses on whole unit squares; use whole-square shapes and treat part-squares informally (pair two halves) until later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Every touched square counted as one; total inflated on the irregular figure.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the square unit: gives the count as a bare number ('18') without 'square cm'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat an area answer without a square unit as incomplete; build the habit of naming the unit; the counting is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct count, no unit; supplies it only when asked.

responseLevels.gap: Counts the boundary/perimeter, leaves gaps or overlaps, or gives a bare number with no square unit.
responseLevels.full: Systematically counts every covering unit square once (decomposing the L-shape), handles part-squares sensibly, compares areas by their counts, and states the area in square units.
responseLevels.partial: Counts the covering squares correctly for a plain rectangle but loses systematicity on the L-shape (double-counts or misses) or mishandles part-squares — succeeds in the clean case but not the irregular one.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a few figures on squared paper — a plain rectangle, an L-shape, and one with part-squares at the edge — plus a book cover and square-centimetre tiles. Say: 'Find the area of each by counting.' Watch whether they count the covering squares or the boundary, whether they cover with no gaps/overlaps and count systematically, what they do with part-squares, and whether they state the unit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands area counts the interior covering squares once each and names the square unit; a child who does not counts the boundary, leaves gaps/overlaps, double-counts on the L-shape, treats part-squares as whole, or drops the unit — each visible in the counting.
